claims.text: Adding a small amount of vanadium to a refractory high-entropy alloy will enhance its radiation tolerance.
Vanadium addition will maintain the alloy's mechanical integrity under fusion-reactor plasma-facing conditions.
The unmodified baseline may be a tungsten-tantalum or similar refractory alloy without vanadium.
The intervention is to introduce a trace amount of vanadium into the refractory high-entropy alloy.
The proposed effect should occur during krypton-ion or similar ion irradiation at fluxes and temperatures representative of fusion plasma-facing environments.
Vanadium addition will cause finely dispersed vanadium-rich clusters or coherent precipitates to form.
Vanadium-rich clusters or coherent precipitates will act as defect sinks.
Vanadium addition promotes the nucleation of defect-absorbing sites.
The defect-absorbing sites facilitate recombination and annihilation of irradiation-induced point defects.
Enhanced point-defect recombination will limit irradiation-induced defect accumulation.
Limiting defect accumulation will preserve microstructural integrity without degrading mechanical properties.
The vanadium-alloyed material will exhibit lower irradiation-induced defect density than the unmodified alloy.
The vanadium-alloyed material may exhibit less swelling or fewer dislocation loops than the unmodified alloy.
The vanadium-alloyed material will retain the baseline alloy's mechanical strength.
The vanadium-alloyed material will retain the baseline alloy's ductility.
The beneficial effect is limited to vanadium concentrations low enough to avoid significant phase instability.
The beneficial effect is limited to vanadium concentrations low enough to avoid mechanical embrittlement.
The optimal vanadium concentration and its redistribution kinetics during irradiation are uncertain.
Vanadium addition may entail mechanical-property trade-offs under extreme conditions.
